## §6 supplement: a component-omitting `DateType` has ONE formal cause, an exact separator in both directions, and a leap-capable yearless day (tri-engine differential, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf196"></a>

> Fold: folded → §6.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-15`, **accepted**; no interpreter defect. [KF176](#kf176) already owned the shape, the whitelist, the extractor gate and the completion, so three of the entry's deltas are consolidations. Two things were genuinely missing, and one was a **stale count in our own prose**.

**The stale count, fixed in place.** KF176's prose named four omitting formats; its own lock (`IncompleteDateFormatAdmissionLawsTest`) has carried `MM-dd` as a fifth since 2026-08-19, and `StructuralKernelFix`'s date-format hint lists five. Two of this repository's three surfaces were right and the canonical one was not — the shape a peer entry is most useful for catching, since a stale prose count is invisible to every guard that reads the lock.

**One cause covers every spelling failure, and the position-in-time cause never arises.** A wrong component width (`yyyy` ← `20`), a text carrying components the format omits (`MM` ← `06-15`), an out-of-range month (`yyyy-MM` ← `2020-13`), and an unreal month-day (`MM-dd` ← `02-30`) all report **`datumFormatFalsch`**. That is structural rather than incidental: no complete date is present to fall below the Gregorian floor, which is exactly why complete-format input needs two causes and these need one.

**The negative existential carries its positive control**, because "the second cause never arises" is satisfied equally by a fixture where it fires nowhere. The same model's complete-format sibling still draws **`datumFalsch`** on `1583-10-15` and is clean on `1583-10-16`, so the second cause is live in the fixture and simply unreachable for the five.

**The separator is exact in BOTH directions.** `yyyy-MM` rejects `202006` and `yyyyMM` rejects `2020-06`, each measured beside the other's accepted canonical text. Either direction alone is satisfied by one lenient parser tolerating an optional dash; the pair is what makes them two formats. This is the *value*-level sibling of KF176's declaration-level separator discriminator (`yyyy-MM` admitted, `yyyy/MM` refused).

**A yearless day is leap-capable and bounded by the month's GREATEST possible day.** `02-29` is accepted and `02-30` refused, so the day is not validated against any particular year's February; `04-31` is refused against `04-30` and `01-31` accepted, so the bound is per month rather than a flat 31. It is the same yearless bound the DateRange overlap rule already uses, measured on this carrier rather than transferred. Empty stored text stays present and value-free on all five.

**Comparison needs no rule of its own** — it is [§6](KERNEL-SEMANTICS.md#6-dates-and-time)'s ordinary coarse gate, and the six measured rows all follow from it: `yyyy == yyyy-MM` and `yyyy == yyyy-MM-dd` are admitted (component sets need not agree), `MM == MM-dd` is admitted (both yearless), and `MM-dd == yyyy`, `MM-dd == yyyy-MM-dd`, `MM == yyyy-MM` are `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE` (year presence differs, no Base Year). Recorded as a consolidation so a reader does not invent a per-format rule.

**On the "interval" reading.** The peer states such a value denotes an interval — a whole year, or a whole month — rather than a day. That is a denotation, not a comparison rule, and the two must not be conflated: measured here, a direct comparison completes the value to the interval's **earliest** date (KF176's completion table), so the interval is not observable through comparison at all.

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.IncompleteDateFormatCauseDiffTest` — twelve rows on the real kernel and the interpreter: the all-canonical and all-empty vacuity controls, the four single-cause failures, both separator directions, the three yearless-day bound rows, and the complete-format positive control for `datumFalsch`. The five-format whitelist stays in `validate.laws.IncompleteDateFormatAdmissionLawsTest`; the six comparison rows are the same file's `theseFormatsCompareThroughTheOrdinaryYearPresenceGate` table.)*

## §13 supplement: the rule error-text checker runs per DECLARED locale, so an undeclared one is stored unchecked (measured, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf197"></a>

> Fold: pending — newly recorded error-text fact; folds into §13 (error-message interpolation) on the next canonical KERNEL-SEMANTICS pass.

Measured with its control, on one model declaring `en_US` + `de_DE`, through `rule add --dry-run` (whose gate is the real `checkConsistency`):

| the message's locale | the text | kernel verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `en_US` (declared) | `See $Nonexistent$` | **rejected** `INVALID_ENTITY` |
| `fr_FR` (undeclared) | `See $Nonexistent$` | **accepted**, no diagnostic |
| `fr_FR` (undeclared) | a well-formed text | accepted, no diagnostic |

The two `fr_FR` rows differ only in whether the text is legal and neither is reported, so the checker is not merely lenient about that locale — it never examines it. The model stays kernel-valid either way, so this is not a legal-model rejection: it is a **silent storage of unchecked text**, and a consumer that offers an author a per-locale message box for an undeclared locale gives them no feedback at all.

**What follows for a candidate checker.** `RuleValidator` injects a placeholder error text per declared locale (so `MVK_ERROR_MESSAGE_MISSING` cannot mask the condition diagnostics), and a supplied message replaces its locale's placeholder. A message for an *undeclared* locale has no placeholder to replace and would simply not be injected anywhere the checker looks — so `rule check --message fr_FR=…` is **refused** (`RK_UNDECLARED_MESSAGE_LOCALE`) rather than answered, because a `valid:true` about a text nothing examined is the one answer that route must not give. That is a deliberate client-side strictness over a model the kernel accepts, and the table above is its measured basis.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.ErrorTextLocaleScopeLawsTest` — the kernel rows, as a within-model pair differing only in the message's locale, plus the indistinguishability row that makes "unexamined" a measurement rather than an inference and the placeholder-merge row. `cli.rule.RuleCheckMessageTest` locks the CLI half: the refusal and its declared-locale twin.)*

## §13 supplement: the rule-message parameter surface — a category suffix, a Base Year terminal, an index-gated key, a narrower quoting rule, and five bilingual terminals (kernel + tri-engine, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf198"></a>

> Fold: pending — newly recorded error-text fact; folds into §13 (error-message interpolation) on the next canonical KERNEL-SEMANTICS pass.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-24-01`, **accepted with three corrections**. §13 named only `$Field$`, `$Field.value$` and `$$`; a rule-owned parameter is four further things besides. The entry also exposed **three interpreter defects**, all fixed here — see the closing note.

**The Enumeration category suffix and its three ordered gates.** `$Field->Category$` is a fourth parameter form, and the two suffixes are **alternatives** rather than decorations: combining them fails to parse in either order.

| parameter | verdict |
|---|---|
| `$Tier->Band$` (declared category) | **admitted** |
| `$Tier->Nope$` | `INVALID_CATEGORY` |
| `$Tier->$` | `NO_CATEGORY` |
| `$Premium->Band$` (not an Enumeration) | `FIELD_NO_ENUM` |
| `$Tier.value->Band$` / `$Tier->Band.value$` | `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN` |

**Correction to the peer entry: a doubled arrow has no single class.** Its first version called the shape a parse failure and its correction said the category gate reports first. Measured, which gate reports depends on the **first name**: `$Tier->Band->Band$` (declared) draws `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN`, `$Tier->Nope->Nope$` draws `INVALID_CATEGORY`, and `$Premium->Band->Band$` draws `FIELD_NO_ENUM`. Each statement is true of one row and neither generalizes; only the three rows together say what the gate order is.

**What the category form is exempt from is the value suffix's NON-STARRED gate, not field membership.** Against one condition whose only reference to the field is starred, the three forms split — and the class the value suffix draws is its own:

| parameter, one starred-only condition | verdict |
|---|---|
| `$Claims/Severity$` | **admitted** |
| `$Claims/Severity.value$` | `PARAM_VALUE_WITH_STARREFERENCE` |
| `$Claims/Severity->Band$` | **admitted** |

Membership still binds every field form alike: with a condition that never names the field, both `$Tier$` and `$Tier->Band$` draw `INVALID_FIELD`. So "neither of the value suffix's extra gates" must be read as *non-starred* + *value-validation*, never as an exemption from membership.

**The quoting rule is narrower than the condition language's, and the two grammars are separately observable.** A field named `For` must be quoted in the *condition* (`FieldFilled('For')` — `FieldFilled(For)` is `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN`) **and** again in the message; a field named `index` must be quoted in neither. The exempt terminals are value, root-group index, line, USB, form-line, form-name, and `index`.

| parameter | verdict |
|---|---|
| `$index$` unquoted / `$'index'$` | **admitted** / **admitted** (the quote is transparent) |
| `$For$` unquoted / `$'For'$` | `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN` / **admitted** |

That exemption also settles the disambiguation §13 left open: `value` is not among the names a field may end with unquoted, so `$Premium.value$` is field + suffix and never a field named `Premium.value`.

**The Base Year terminal.** A parameter need not be a field: `$BaseYear$` with an optional signed offset is gated only on the model declaring a Base Year, with no bound on the offset.

| parameter | verdict |
|---|---|
| `$BaseYear$`, `$BaseYear+3$`, `$BaseYear-1$`, `$BaseYear+9999$` | **admitted** |
| `$BaseYear$` with no Base Year declared | `NO_BASE_YEAR` |
| `$BaseYear+$` / `$BaseYear+x$` / `$BaseYear 3$` | `MVK_EXPECTED_TOKEN_NOT_FOUND` / `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN` / `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN` |

**The semantic-index key is gated on the INDEX, not on the field — the load-bearing pair.** Against a condition reading only `Claims/Payout For "C-1"`, a keyed parameter naming the group's **index field** is admitted while the unkeyed spelling of that same field is refused. Every refusing row quotes a field and a key together, so only the admitted row separates the two accounts.

**Corrected 2026-09-05 — that clause read "a *different* field of that group", which is wider than its only witness.** `ClaimNo` is the group's declared `indexField`, so across every row of the original table "any field of the group, once keyed" and "the keyed field, or the index" moved together and could not be told apart. The discriminator is a **third** field — neither named by the condition nor the index — and it is REFUSED `MVK_INDEX_FOR_ERROR_TEXT_INVALID`, measured on the same fixture, which happens to carry `Claims/Severity`. So the admitted set at a keyed parameter is *the field the condition keys, or the group's index field*, not the group's fields at large. Found by authoring the construct through `dmtool` for a12-kernel-lean, who could not reach it at all and asked how; the row that answers their question is the row that falsified ours.

| condition | parameter | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| keyed `Claims/Payout For "C-1"` | `$Claims/ClaimNo For "C-1"$` (field absent from the condition) | **admitted** |
| the same | `$Claims/ClaimNo$` | `INVALID_FIELD` |
| the same | `$Claims/Payout For "C-9"$` (different key) | `MVK_INDEX_FOR_ERROR_TEXT_INVALID` |
| plain per-row read | `$Payout For "C-1"$` (beside its admitted unkeyed control) | `MVK_INDEX_FOR_ERROR_TEXT_INVALID` |
| field-keyed `For Adjuster` | `$… For Adjuster$` / `$… For "C-1"$` | **admitted** / `MVK_INDEX_FOR_ERROR_TEXT_INVALID` |

The key comes **last**: `$Claims/Payout.value For "C-1"$` is admitted, `$… For "C-1".value$` is `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN`. *(A fifth parameter form this enumeration did not reach — `$index(…).value$`, which pins a message to the firing row's declared index-field value — is [KF275](#kf275).)* It is a quoted literal or a field path, so an unquoted bare word is a field reference (`INVALID_ENTITY`), and a key that is itself keyed is `ILLEGAL_SEMANTIC_INDEX`.

**The grammar is bilingual, five terminals differ, and the other language's spelling is a WRONG VALUE risk rather than a syntax error.** The terminals follow the model's declared **condition language**, not its display locale (a `de_DE`-locale model still parses English conditions until `modelConfig.conditionLanguage` says otherwise). Five differ — value/`Wert`, `For`/`Fuer`, `RuleGroup`/`RegelKontext`, `RootGroup`/`LfdNr`, `BaseYear`/`Referenzjahr` — while `index`, `Zeile`, `Usb`, `Vordruckzeile` and `Vordruckname` are spelled the same, and the bundle's own comments record that **`Zeile` and `Usb` are not permitted in an A12 model**. Measured in both directions:

| terminal, position | own language | other language |
|---|---|---|
| value / `Wert` (name) | **admitted** | `INVALID_ENTITY` |
| `BaseYear` / `Referenzjahr` (name) | **admitted** | `INVALID_ENTITY` |
| `RuleGroup` / `RegelKontext` (name) | `INVALID_PARAMETER` | `INVALID_ENTITY` |
| `For` / `Fuer` (keyword) | **admitted** | `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN` |

The rule-group pair is the sharpest instrument: neither spelling is admitted at a rule-owned parameter, but the own-language one is **recognised** and refused in this position while the other's is **looked up as a field**. That is the mechanism behind the wrong-value risk, measured rather than assumed — a model declaring a field of that name would silently resolve the field. The `For`/`Fuer` pair sits in keyword position, fails to parse, and therefore carries no such risk.

**`RootGroup`/`LfdNr` is not reachable from a rule-owned parameter at all.** Both spellings draw `INVALID_ENTITY` in both languages, at a scalar locus and at an iterating one, with and without a repeatable root group — on the same fixtures where the rule-group pair separates as the positive control. Stated as a measured absence, not as a claim about the terminal bundle, which is shared across parameter owners.

**What they RENDER**, byte-identically on both kernel codegen strategies and now on the interpreter. Two rows are within-model controls because the obvious statement is fixture-true rather than general, and one of them **corrects the peer entry**:

| message | rendered |
|---|---|
| `$Tier->Band$` with `Tier` holding `BASIC` | `STANDARD` — the category TOKEN, not the category name, not the stored value |
| `$Tier.value$`, `BASIC` **labelled** "Basic cover" | `Basic cover` — the LABEL |
| `$RawTier.value$`, `BASIC` **unlabelled**, same document | `BASIC` — the stored token |
| `$Tier->Band$` / `$Tier.value$` on an empty Enumeration | `` / `` — while `$Tier$` still renders `Tier` |
| `$BaseYear$` `$BaseYear+3$` `$BaseYear-1$` `$$` against a declared 2020 | `2020` `2023` `2019` `$` |
| `$Premium.value$`, unfilled, **max** 2 fractional digits | `0` |
| `$MinPremium.value$`, unfilled, **min** 2 fractional digits, same document | `0.00` |
| `$Reference$` unlabelled / `$Handler$` labelled, same document | `Reference` / `Claims handler` |

**Two corrections to the peer's rendered clause, both fixture-true there.** It states that `$Status.value$` renders `open`; measured, an Enumeration's value suffix renders the value's **declared label** and falls back to the stored token only when the declaration carries none — the third row is the discriminator, in one document. And it states that "an unfilled Number declaring two fractional digits renders `0.00`"; the gate is **`minFractionalDigits`**, which §13's own prose already had right, and the sixth and seventh rows separate them in one model. Its short-name and declared-label rows are confirmed as written.

**The three interpreter defects this found.** The tri-engine arm was red on four of the six rendered rows: the category suffix was left in the text as a raw `$Tier->Band$` token, an Enumeration's `.value` rendered the stored token rather than the label, and `$BaseYear$` fell through to an entity lookup and rendered the identifier debug form `/Policy/BaseYear/1.1`. All three are fixed (`FieldDef.enumValueLabels` + `ModelDef.enumValueTextOf`/`enumCategoryTokenOf`, and a language-aware terminal set in `renderMessage`), and the interpreter now agrees with both kernel strategies on every row.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.RuleMessageParameterLawsTest` — the admission tables above, each asserted whole so a kernel upgrade shows the entire matrix rather than its first divergence, and each row preceded by a plain-message control proving the CONDITION is admitted; `validate.laws.RuleMessageParameterLanguageLawsTest` — the bilingual pairs in both directions plus the unreachable root-group pair with its positive control; `adapter.laws.RuleMessageParameterRenderingDiffTest` — the rendered rows on dynamic Groovy, static Java and the interpreter; `interpreter … RuleMessageParameterRenderTest` — the same rendering on JVM and JS, plus the `de_DE` condition language the kernel fixture does not carry.)*

## §13 supplement: a `$field.value$` renders the MESSAGE LOCALE's presentation, for nine tags and no others — and a partial date keeps its markers (tri-engine, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf199"></a>

> Fold: pending — newly recorded error-text fact; folds into §13 (error-message interpolation) on the next canonical KERNEL-SEMANTICS pass.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-09`, **accepted and considerably widened**. Their entry states two facts about DATE; measured here, the mechanism reaches four field kinds, is keyed on an exact locale tag that ordinary spellings MISS, and leaves three things alone that an implementation would helpfully change. It also found a fourth interpreter defect ([IF308](INTERPRETER-FINDINGS.md#if308)).

**The presented value is not the stored value and not the declared format.** One document, one rule, ten message locales; only the locale varies:

| kind, stored as | `en_US` / `en` / `us` | `de_DE` / `de` | `ch` | `fr` | `gb` | `nl` | `fr_FR` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DATE `2024-06-15` (`yyyy-MM-dd`) | `06/15/2024` | `15.06.2024` | `15.06.2024` | `15/06/2024` | `15/06/2024` | `15-06-2024` | **`2024-06-15`** |
| DATE `15.06.2024` (`dd.MM.yyyy`) | `06/15/2024` | `15.06.2024` | … | … | … | … | **`15.06.2024`** |
| NUMBER `1234.50` | `1,234.50` | `1.234,50` | `1'234.50` | `1 234,50` | `1,234.50` | `1.234,50` | **`1234.50`** |
| DATE_TIME `2024-06-15T13:45:00` | `06/15/2024 13:45:00` | `15.06.2024 13:45:00` | … | … | … | … | **`2024-06-15T13:45:00`** |
| DATE_RANGE `2024-06-15/2024-07-01` | `06/15/2024 07/01/2024` | `15.06.2024 01.07.2024` | … | … | … | … | **`2024-06-15/2024-07-01`** |
| TIME `13:45:00` | `13:45:00` | `13:45:00` | `13:45:00` | `13:45:00` | `13:45:00` | `13:45:00` | `13:45:00` |

The second row is the one that shows the declared format is only an INPUT: two DATE fields differing solely in their declared format render identically under a mapped locale and differently under an unmapped one.

**The locale map is a LOOKUP on the exact tag, not a cascade.** The nine keys are `en`, `en_US`, `us`, `de`, `de_DE`, `ch`, `fr`, `gb`, `nl`; **`fr_FR` is not among them**, and it is the ordinary spelling a model declares. A miss presents nothing at all — every value renders as stored. So a consumer that implemented presentation as "the locale's own conventions, with a sensible default" would be right on every mapped row and wrong on the one that occurs in practice. Two keys make the same point from the other side: `ch` pairs the German date pattern with an **apostrophe** grouping separator and a dot decimal, and `gb` pairs a day-first date pattern with the English separators — neither is what a locale library would produce.

**Three deliberate non-effects, each measured, each what "being helpful" would break.**

- **TIME is never re-presented.** Its format is identical in every entry, so a time renders as stored under all ten locales.
- **An unfilled field's DEFAULT is not presented.** A Number declaring two minimum fractional digits renders `0.00` under `de_DE`, whose *filled* values in the same message use a comma. So the default is chosen by the field format downstream of the presentation, which confirms §13's existing sentence rather than contradicting it — the two live side by side in one message here.
- **Fractional digits are preserved, never padded.** A stored `1234.5` in a `min 0 / max 2` field renders `1,234.5`; only the separators change. A negative keeps its sign in front of the grouped integer: `-1,234,567.50`.

**A partially known DATE interpolates its stored components with the zero markers intact, and is never completed.** `2024-06-00` renders `06/00/2024`, `2024-00-00` renders `00/00/2024`, `0000-00-00` renders `00/00/0000`. The natural implementation resolves such a value before display and would print `06/01/2024` — the earliest date of the interval it denotes, and a date the document never stated. The markers **move with the pattern** (`00.06.2024` under `de_DE`), which puts each marker on its COMPONENT rather than on a text position: an implementation that blanked a fixed offset passes every `en_US` row and fails the German ones.

**The two separators the presentation replaces are worth naming.** A DATE_TIME's `T` becomes a space, and a DATE_RANGE's declared separator (`/` in the fixture) becomes a space too — both fixed across every locale entry rather than per-locale slots.

*Mechanism (hypothesis, not measured): the kernel's per-locale presentation record is fetched by exact `Locale` key and passed to the field's own conversion, and a null record makes the conversion return the value unchanged. That reading explains the miss and the fallback together; what stands is the table.*

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.MessageDisplayPresentationDiffTest` — all ten locales over one document carrying every kind, on dynamic Groovy, static Java and the interpreter, with the unmapped `fr_FR` row and the unpadded/negative/unfilled rows as the controls; `interpreter … MessageDisplayPresentationTest` — the same on JVM and Node, including the partial-date markers under two patterns.)*

## §6 supplement: the DateRange overlap operators have TWO admission gates, and neither is the equality gate (kernel + tri-engine, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf200"></a>

> Fold: folded → §6.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-22-01` and `SPEC-2026-08-23-01`, **both accepted**; no interpreter defect. They are recorded together because their whole value is that they are *different gates on the same operators*, and a reader who merges them gets both wrong.

**Gate 1 — year class, over the whole authored list.** Every operand carries the year or none does; a mix is `MVK_DATE_WITH_AND_WITHOUT_YEAR`. A declared **Base Year lifts it**.

| condition, one model | no Base Year | Base Year 2024 |
|---|---|---|
| `DateRangesOverlap(yyyy-MM-dd, yyyy)` — both year-bearing, **different component sets** | **admitted** | admitted |
| `DateRangesOverlap(MM, MM-dd)` — both yearless, different component sets | **admitted** | admitted |
| `DateRangesOverlap(yyyy-MM-dd, MM)`, and the reverse order | `MVK_DATE_WITH_AND_WITHOUT_YEAR` | **admitted** |
| three operands, one of them mixed | same | **admitted** |
| `AtLeastOneDateRangeOverlaps(scalar In list*)`, mixed **across** the two sides | same | **admitted** |

The first two rows are what separate this gate from the equality one ([KF's §6 comparability entry](#kf193)): equality requires *equal component sets* and overlap does not. Conflating them refuses lists the kernel admits.

**Gate 2 — an `interpretationOfYear` declaration is refused outright.** `MVK_INVALID_DATE_RANGE_FORMAT`, on either side of `DateRangesOverlap`, on either side of the plural operator, and **with or without a Base Year** — a property of the declaration, not of the value. Its interpretation-FREE twin — same format, same separator, same year class, same model — is admitted, which is what makes the declaration the variable.

**And the second gate is confined to those two operators.** The same interpretation-bearing declaration is admitted by `StartOfDateRange`, `EndOfDateRange` and `==`. Without this row the refusal reads as a blanket ban and a consumer would reject models the kernel accepts.

**Three runtime rows, because two of the admission facts have a meaning a reader would guess wrong.**

- **A Base Year COMPLETES, it does not make the comparison year-blind.** June 2023 against a yearless `06/06` completed to base year 2024 does **not** overlap; the same window in 2024 does. A month-vs-month comparison passes the second row and fails the first.
- **An all-yearless list with no Base Year compares labels directly**, and a month-only endpoint reaches that month's greatest possible last day: a bare `02` overlaps `02-29` and not `03-01`.
- **An interpreted endpoint is checked in the year it is PLACED in.** One stored `01.11-29.02` under Base Year 2020: valid under `TO` (the base year is the to-year, so the leap day is in 2020 and the start rolls back to 2019) and `datumBereichFormatFalsch` under `FROM` (the end rolls forward to 2021, which has no 29 February).

*(Locked: `validate.laws.DateRangeOverlapAdmissionLawsTest` — five verdict tables, each asserted whole, with the interpretation-free twin and the bound-extraction confinement rows as the controls; `adapter.laws.DateRangeOverlapYearClassLawsTest` — the three runtime rows plus an explicit admission assertion for the two spliced models, because two of its rows assert a rule does NOT fire and a refused model would satisfy them vacuously.)*

## §6 supplement: a selected DateRange endpoint carries its declaration's components, and its consumers are gated separately (kernel + runtime, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf201"></a>

> Fold: folded → §6.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-02` and `SPEC-2026-08-23-05`, **accepted with one correction**; no interpreter defect. The two are recorded together because they are one account: what a selected endpoint *is*, and therefore which consumers may read it.

**Extraction is unconditional; the consumers are what is gated.** `StartOfDateRange` and `EndOfDateRange` are admitted on every admitted declaration, including a yearless profile in a model with no Base Year. A checker that required a Base Year before extracting a yearless bound refuses kernel-legal models.

**Gate 1 — the numeric extractor reads the declaration's COMPONENT SET.** The full grid, seven profiles × four extractors, with no Base Year (✓ = admitted, ✗ = `MVK_WRONG_DATE_FORMAT_FOR_OP`):

| declaration | Year | Month | Day | Quarter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dd.MM.yyyy`, `yyyy-MM-dd` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `yyyy` | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| `yyyy-MM` | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ |
| `MM` | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ |
| `MM-dd`, `dd.MM` | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

Quarter rides the month, cell for cell. **A declared Base Year supplements YEAR and only YEAR:** the three `✗` in the Year column flip to `✓` and *no other cell moves* — asserted as a diff between the two grids, with `Day of MM` staying refused in the configured model as the live control. Without that control the row is satisfied by a Base Year that simply admits everything.

**Gate 2 — a comparison uses the ordinary DIRECT temporal rule, with a different code.** Same unconfigured model:

| condition | verdict |
|---|---|
| `MonthFromDate(StartOfDateRange(MM-range)) >= 1` | **admitted** |
| `StartOfDateRange(MM-range) == <complete DATE>` | `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE` |
| `StartOfDateRange(yyyy-range) == <complete DATE>` | **admitted** |
| `StartOfDateRange(MM) == StartOfDateRange(MM-dd)` / `== StartOfDateRange(yyyy)` | admitted / `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE` |

Rows one and two on one declaration are what force the two gates apart; stating one gate for both consumers is the mistake. **Correction to the peer entry:** it says "a yearless *or year-only* profile with no Base Year is refused" — measured, the **year-only** profile is admitted, because the direct gate asks only for matching **year presence** and `yyyy` carries it. Grouping the two rejects a kernel-legal comparison, and the entry's own appeal to the ordinary direct rule is what predicts the admission.

**The component travels to the computation surface unchanged**, and it is a non-expandable **scale-0** operation there: the month of an unconfigured `MM` range assigns to an integer target, its year is still `MVK_WRONG_DATE_FORMAT_FOR_OP`, and a fractional target draws `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_DEC_PLACES`.

**A ROW endpoint is a sixth member of the rule-locus list, and there the LOCUS gate reports first.** One model, one operand whose profile withholds the requested component, differing only in where the error field sits: a non-iterating error field draws `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` and an iterating one draws `MVK_WRONG_DATE_FORMAT_FOR_OP`. A starred occurrence is `MVK_NO_WILDCARDS_ALLOWED`, so an iterating rule is the only legal way to read a row endpoint's component.

**Four runtime rows, because a reader that passed every gate above can still resolve the wrong value.**

- **Completion is POSITIONAL.** A month-only start completes to the first of its month, so it equals a month-and-day start exactly when that day is `01` — and not when it is `02`. The pair separates positional completion from a month-wide comparison.
- **An unconfigured yearless range computes its RETAINED label** — a `MM` range's month is a real number with no Base Year anywhere in the model, so the reading does not depend on completion.
- **An unplaced range computes the real number `0`**, not "no value". A caller treating zero as absent reads it wrong.
- **A formally invalid range clears its reader's target while a clean sibling still computes** in the same row. The sibling is the control: without it, "cleared" is satisfied by a document that computes nothing at all.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.DateRangeBoundComponentLawsTest` — the unconditional-extraction row, both grids asserted whole with the Base-Year diff and its day control, the two comparison tables, the computation surface with its scale rule, and the locus order including a raw-string starred row the typed builder deliberately cannot express; `adapter.laws.DateRangeBoundComponentValueLawsTest` — the four runtime rows with the positional pair and the computing sibling as controls.)*

## §6/§11 supplement: a DATE_RANGE computation's two gates are ORDERED, and both spellings of a component set participate (kernel + runtime, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf202"></a>

> Fold: folded → §6.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-03`, **accepted as stated**; it corrects prose of ours, amended in place above.

**The two gates read different things.** The **operand list** must share one lexical DECLARATION PROFILE; the **target** is decided by the date-COMPONENT SET. Because `dd.MM.yyyy`+`-` and `yyyy-MM-dd`+`/` are two profiles of one component set, a single model separates them:

| computation | verdict |
|---|---|
| `FirstFilledValue(Eu, Eu)` → ISO target | **admitted** |
| `FirstFilledValue(Iso, Iso)` → ISO target | **admitted** |
| `FirstFilledValue(Eu, Iso)` → ISO target | `MVK_VARYING_TYPES_NOT_ALLOWED` |
| `FirstFilledValue(Eu, Eu, Iso)` → ISO target | `MVK_VARYING_TYPES_NOT_ALLOWED` |
| `FirstFilledValue(MonthSlash, Eu)` → month target | `MVK_VARYING_TYPES_NOT_ALLOWED` |
| `FirstFilledValue(MonthSlash, MonthSlash)` → ISO target | `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE_RANGE` |
| `FirstFilledValue(Eu, Eu)` → month target | `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE_RANGE` |

**Row five is the ordering row.** It is the only row where BOTH gates would refuse — the list mixes component sets *and* the second source cannot reach the target — and the kernel reports the list class **alone**, with no target class beside it (the verdict joins every code the kernel emits, so a co-firing second gate would show). The consequence for a consumer is a repair hint that points at the wrong thing: change the target, rather than change the odd source. *Rows three and four are NOT ordering evidence, which is worth saying because they read like it: their sources all share the target's component set, so the target gate would pass and a target-first checker reaches the list gate and answers identically. They measure that the list gate reads the lexical profile — which is their own job — and the first version of this entry mislabelled row four as the discriminator.*

**Both spellings of each component set participate on either side, on both shapes.** Measured admitted: an empty-separator `MM` list into a slash `MM` target and the reverse; a slash `MM-dd` list into a dotted `dd.MM` target; a `MM` construction into either month target; a `MM-dd` construction into the dotted day-month target. A `MM-dd` construction into a `MM` target is `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE_RANGE`, so the crossing is inside one component set and not a general relaxation. The yearless spellings are the ones that matter here: an implementation enumerating one spelling per component set cannot express a `MM`+`""` or `dd.MM`+`-` target at all.

**And the target's own spelling renders the stored text.** The `{YEAR, MONTH, DAY}` crossing was already locked (`DateRangeFirstFilledProfileDiffTest.theTargetFormatDecidesTheStoredForm`, storing `2024-06-01/2024-06-30` from a dotted source). The yearless crossing is new and reaches a different read path — `MM`+`""` is the one declaration whose stored text splits in the MIDDLE rather than on a separator — and it is measured on a **direct two-field list** so the second slot is separable from ordinary row order: a stored `0609` in the first source computes `06/09`, and with the first source empty a `0110` in the second computes `01/10`.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.DateRangeComputationGateOrderLawsTest` — the ordering table, the uniform-list target table, and both crossing tables with same-spelling controls; `adapter.laws.DateRangeCrossedSpellingComputeDiffTest` — the admission assertion plus the two rendered rows and an all-empty clear.)*

## §11 supplement: a computation operand is admitted by the target's scope BINDING its levels, and is read at its own path (kernel + runtime, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf203"></a>

> Fold: folded → §11.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-06`, **accepted with one correction**; no interpreter defect.

**Confirmed: the gate is binding, not scope equality.** An operand at or above the target's repetition scope is admitted — a form-level operand into a one-level target, a form-level operand into a two-level target, and a middle-level operand into a two-level target all pass. A repeatable level the target's coordinates cannot address is refused `MVK_NO_WILDCARD`: one level BELOW the target, and a repeatable operand feeding a form-level target. The starred aggregate is the admitted flattening route over that deeper group, which is what stops the refusal reading as a ban on depth. Measured across five operand shapes — a bare reference, `Length`, `MonthFromDate`, `Abs`, and a mixed outer-plus-row arithmetic pair — so it is the scope gate and not an operand-kind rule. A checker built on scope equality rejects every computation that reads a form-level constant into a row.

**The correction: a SIBLING repeatable operand is not one verdict, and it is not `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` in general.** It is the kernel's **parallel-iteration** route, and the answer is decided by the sibling group's index-field declaration. Target and operand shape held fixed, only that declaration varying:

| the sibling group declares | verdict |
|---|---|
| an index field with **another** name | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_INVALID_INDEX` |
| an index field with the **same** name as the target's group | **admitted** — a legal parallel iteration |
| **no** index field | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` |
| — read through a starred aggregate instead | **admitted** |

The peer clause states the third row as the whole class. **The three rows above ARE the discriminating case**: a rival account in which siblinghood itself is refused predicts a refusal on row two, and row two is admitted — the only variable between them is the index-field name. That identifies the gate as [KF67](#kf67)'s authoring precondition for parallel iteration, reached here from the computation surface: the iterated group's index field must carry the same name as the index field on the computed field's path. So the sibling case and the below-the-target case are different mechanisms that merely share a diagnostic on the index-free reading, and a fixture whose groups carry differently-named index fields measures the index gate while looking exactly like a measurement of siblinghood — the trap [KF186](#kf186) records on the `RepetitionNotUnique` carrier.

**The runtime half, which an admission test cannot see.** Each operand is read at **its own path inside the current target row**. An implementation that derives the operand's address from the target's path finds nothing there and reads it as empty on every row — a wrong VALUE rather than a refusal, and on a NUMBER operand the substituted zero makes it look plausible. Five rows, all three engines agreeing:

- one root cell reaches every target row **as a value** (`10` → `90`, `190`), **as a substituted zero** when empty (`100`, `200`), and **as a clear** when formally invalid (both rows cleared);
- with a **two-level** target and the operand at the middle level, two enclosing rows carrying different values give **their own** leaves different results (`105`, `107` under the first; `205` under the second) — a target-path read gives all three the same answer;
- an invalid enclosing operand **clears only its own leaves**, the clean sibling row still computing.

Every target row is seeded, because an untouched target reports no change at all rather than CLEARED and the clear rows would otherwise be vacuous.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.ComputationOperandScopeLawsTest` — the binding table, the below-the-target table, the starred-aggregate route, the three-cell sibling index-name control, and the five-shape spread; `adapter.laws.ComputationOperandOwnPathDiffTest` — the five runtime rows on dynamic Groovy, static Java and the interpreter.)*

## §9 supplement: the operand-locus gate reports FIRST, and every DateRange carrier obeys it (kernel, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf204"></a>

> Fold: folded → §9.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-04`, **accepted as stated**, with one extension.

**The gate order.** Both gates on an authored rule were separately documented; which one reports was not. Measured with a two-row separator on one model:

| rule | verdict |
|---|---|
| unstarred repeatable operand **+** an error field the condition never names | `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` |
| the same unreferenced error field, scalar operands only | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_REFERENCED` |
| the same condition with the error field referenced — control | admitted |

Row two is what makes row one an ordering fact: remove only the repeatable operand and the error-field gate speaks. A checker that runs the error-field gate first sends the author to fix the wrong half of the condition.

**Extension — the locus gate outranks the ARITY gate too.** A sole bare operand of the whole-list overlap operator is `MVK_PARAMSIZE_INVALIDFN` from an iterating locus and `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` from a non-iterating one. Same rule, same operand, only the error field moved.

**Five DateRange carriers, measured rather than transferred.** The overlap predicate, stored range equality, an extracted endpoint against a fixed Date, an endpoint pair, and the two-endpoint construction are each admitted from an iterating locus and refused `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` from a non-iterating one, every row carrying a presence guard on its own locus's error field so only the locus gate can speak. They agree — which is a result, not a licence to transfer the rule to a sixth carrier without running it.

**The overlap operators, in detail.** For the whole-list operator the *list shape* is locus-independent and the *bare operand* is not: lengths two and three behave alike, a starred occurrence is admitted from either locus, and a list carrying both the bare and the starred spelling of one field is admitted from inside. The distinguished-scalar operator obeys the rule on **both** of its sides — a repeatable distinguished scalar against a scalar list, and a scalar against a repeatable list.

**And the negative-condition-in-iteration gate is presence-shaped, not polarity-shaped.** On one model, one locus and one error field, varying only the condition: an unguarded negative *presence* on the iterated operand is `MVK_NEG_CONDITION_IN_ITERATION`, its guarded twin is admitted, and stored range equality, its inequality, an extracted-endpoint equality, its inequality and an order comparison are all admitted. The refused row is the live control — without it the admitted comparisons could be a fixture that has stopped checking.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.RuleLocusGateOrderLawsTest` — the ordering separator, the five carriers, the negative-gate reach with its live control, and both overlap operators including the two sole-operand rows.)*

## §6/§9 supplement: a DATE_RANGE operand may be selected by a semantic index (kernel + runtime, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf205"></a>

> Fold: folded → §6.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-07`, **accepted with one correction**; it exposed a typed-surface gap of ours, now closed.

**The keyed operand is admitted wherever the direct field is.** Four carriers — an extracted endpoint, that endpoint's numeric component, stored range equality, and an endpoint pair — × two key forms (literal and field-keyed) × two loci, including the sharp one where the rule **iterates the very group the lookup keys into**: sixteen admitted rows. A checker reading the endpoint operand as "a direct field" rejects kernel-legal models on four carriers at once.

**Our typed surface could not express it at all.** `DateRangeRef` was the one typed ref *of a kind the kernel indexes* without `forIndex`, so the keyed range cell was *unrepresentable* rather than refused — the type-level form of the same defect, and exactly the shape the "a client-side refusal needs a measured kernel basis" rule warns about. Closed by `DateRangeRef.forIndex` returning a `DateRangeIndexedValue`, its own arm of `DateRangeOperand` so that `Dsl.startOfDateRange(DateRangeIndexedValue)` can exist without also admitting `StartOfDateRange(FirstFilledValue(…))` — **measured 2026-08-24**, that nested form is `MVK_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN`, so the narrower type is not a precaution but the shape of the gate.

**The wildcard half, measured for this carrier.** A **starred** endpoint operand is `MVK_NO_WILDCARDS_ALLOWED` at **either** locus — so no wildcard form of it exists, and an iterating rule or a keyed lookup are the only two ways to reach a per-row endpoint. A **group** operand is `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` instead.

**Two key rules with their own classes.** A field-valued key read from **inside** the indexed group is `MVK_SEMANTIC_INDEX_CONTAINED_IN_INDEX`, against admitted outside-key and literal-key twins at the same locus — so it is a *placement* rule, not a resolution failure. And the literal key is a **quoted** token whatever the index field's kind: against a NUMBER index field `For 2` is `MVK_INVALID_ENTITY` (an entity that does not resolve) while `For "2"` is admitted, and a quoted literal that does not fit the declaration is the separate `MVK_INDEX_VALUE_INVALID`.

**The four read states, separated by a presence operand.** With the absence and presence rules run as a pair on the same document (`<absence fires>/<presence fires>`), on both kernel strategies and the interpreter:

| the keyed cell is | absence / presence | reading |
|---|---|---|
| matched and filled | `false/true` | a value |
| a clean no-match | `true/false` | **empty** |
| matched but empty | `true/false` | **empty** |
| a duplicated key | `false/false` | **UNKNOWN** |
| matched but formally invalid | `false/false` | **UNKNOWN** |

The presence column is what tells the pairs apart; the absence column alone cannot. The duplicate additionally reports `uniqueIndex` on **each** participating index cell.

**Correction to the peer entry — the negative row coordinate is a KNOWN sentinel, not an invented address.** An unguarded keyed negative presence escapes the negative-condition-in-iteration gate (a keyed lookup is not an iterated read), is admitted, and fires once at `/Shop/Runs/RunWindow, [1, -5, 1]`. The peer records this as "a negative row coordinate, which no legal address holds", and advises refusing the shape. Measured, the coordinate is **-5** — the kernel's clean-no-match reanchoring sentinel that [KERNEL-SEMANTICS §9](KERNEL-SEMANTICS.md#9-repetition-iteration-and-cross-array-evaluation) already records for message-pointer targeting. So the address is readable: a consumer maps `-5` to "no matching row" rather than inventing a coordinate or rejecting the rule. The guarded twin and a guarded direct-operand control both address a real row on the same document — and the twin's error field is forced to be a *directly* iterated field, because once a guard puts the rule into iteration the kernel demands an iterating reference to the error field (`MVK_ERROR_FIELD_AND_ITERATION_INVALID`), which a keyed lookup is not. That is the same fact the escape exploits, seen from the other side.

**The READ half, added the same day after a cold review, because the authoring half alone was not the capability.** The converter could read neither side of a keyed range, and the two sides failed differently: on the LEFT of a comparison it threw and degraded the rule to `Opaque` — loud, and merely unreadable — while on the RIGHT it built a bare `DateRangeRef` and **silently dropped the key**, so the rule round-tripped to a different, still-legal condition that reported itself `Converted`. That second one is the wrong-value failure, and it is the exact shape of the class this project already records twice ([KF193](#kf193)'s "a legal model was unreadable, not merely unauthorable"; the enum-category erasure that shipped from two different sites). Both sides now thread the key, and the drop has the same backstop the `$` correlation and the category projection already had — a dropped key degrades the subject to a verbatim `Opaque` instead of corrupting it.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.DateRangeSemanticIndexOperandLawsTest` — the sixteen-row admission grid, both wildcard refusals, the contained-key class with two twins, and the three key-literal rows; `adapter.laws.KeyedRangeReadStateDiffTest` — the four-state table on all three engines, the duplicate's per-cell reports, and the escape's exact address beside its two controls; `adapter.KeyedRangeReadBackTest` — both operand sides and the field-keyed form round-tripping with their key, an unkeyed control that must not gain one, and the backstop's does-fire/does-not-fire pair.)*

## §6 supplement: the temporal FORMAT gate is a kind-independent vocabulary (kernel, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf206"></a>

> Fold: not-foldable — an authoring-tier declaration rule, like [KF81](#kf81) which it corrects.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-10`, **accepted as stated**. It corrects the framing of [KF81](#kf81), which is ours.

**KF81 enumerated the admitted formats per KIND** — "DATE: both `yyyy-MM-dd` and `dd.MM.yyyy`; TIME: the full `HH:mm:ss` is required; DATE_TIME: the only date-bearing format is ISO" — and every cell it ran sat inside its own kind's column. A per-kind allowlist and a single shared vocabulary predict identical results on that grid, so the enumeration was complete in one direction and untested in the other. Measured across the kinds, the gate validates the **string** and never consults the kind.

**The discriminating pair, on one field of one kind:** a TIME field is **refused** `HH:mm` — a natural spelling for its kind — and **admitted** `yyyy-MM-dd`, which is not one. No kind-keyed gate produces that pair.

The cross-admissions: `HH:mm:ss` and the ISO datetime format on **DATE**; `yyyy-MM-dd`, `dd.MM.yyyy` and the fragment format `MM` on **TIME**. Each kind's own default is admitted as a control, and each kind's default is therefore not a restriction. The negative half is what makes it a *vocabulary* rather than an absence of checking: nine unrecognized strings are refused at the model level — `HH:mm`, `H:mm:ss`, `HH:mm:ss.SSS`, `hh:mm:ss a`, `HHmmss` and `HH-mm-ss` on TIME, and three space-separated datetime spellings on DATE_TIME. An admitted mismatch survives our own model serialization unchanged. *Whether the KERNEL re-emits it unnormalized is the peer's measurement (`field read`), carried forward rather than reproduced here — our row asserts the builder's output, which a kernel-side normalization would not touch.*

**What this does not say.** Static admission only. What a mismatched declaration stores, renders, or is admitted as an operand is a separate question — characterized for the degenerate time-only DATE_TIME in [KF81](#kf81) and untouched here. A consumer must not infer a component set from a field's kind **in either direction**.

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.TemporalFormatVocabularyLawsTest` — the discriminating pair, the cross-admission witnesses with per-kind controls, the nine refusals, and the unnormalized read-back. Its `verdict` deliberately has no `catch`: an exception would be a CLIENT-side refusal, and letting it propagate is what keeps a builder throw from being reported as a kernel rejection.)*

## §6 supplement: which formal cause a rejected temporal input carries (kernel + runtime, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf207"></a>

> Fold: folded → §6.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-08` and `-11`, **both accepted as stated**; `-11` found an interpreter defect ([IF309](INTERPRETER-FINDINGS.md#if309)).

**A partial Date's cause is chosen in two stages.** A **FULL-precision** declaration reports *any* omission marker as `datumFormatFalsch`, because an omission is not a legal spelling for it at all — so one stored text draws different answers from two declarations differing **only** in precision (`2024-02-00` is the format error at FULL and admitted at `DAY_OPTIONAL`; `2024-00-00` likewise against `MONTH_OPTIONAL`). A declaration that admits omissions splits its rejections:

| input at an omission-admitting precision | cause |
|---|---|
| wrong component width (`2024-2-01`) | `datumFormatFalsch` |
| unreal calendar date among the **present** components (`2024-02-31`) | `datumFormatFalsch` |
| a zero pattern that is not a monotone suffix (`2024-00-15` at `MONTH_OPTIONAL`) | `datumFalsch` |
| a suffix deeper than the precision admits (`2024-00-00` at `DAY_OPTIONAL`) | `datumFalsch` |
| earliest completion below the Gregorian floor (`1583-10-00` at `DAY_OPTIONAL`) | `datumFalsch` |

**The gates run reality, then position in time, then precision.** An impossible month beside a legally omitted day (`2024-13-00` at `DAY_OPTIONAL`) is the **format** error — the omission is admitted and the month is not, so the month's cause wins — while `1583-10-00` at the same precision is the **date** error and `1583-11-00` is admitted. The peer records the trap that order creates: an implementation obtaining its partial value through a constructor that applies the floor internally reports the floor case as a format error, because the constructor's "no value" is indistinguishable from unreality.

**Time and DateTime have no codes of their own.** Both report through the **Date** codes. A **Time** cell reaches only the format one — a width violation and every out-of-range component alike. **Corrected 2026-08-28: the deciding variable is the DECLARATION, not the kind** — that holds for a TIME field declared with a *time* format, while one declared `yyyy-MM-dd` does reach `datumFalsch` ([KF211](#kf211)); and hour **24 is not an end-of-day spelling**: `24:00:00` is refused exactly as `25:00:00` is, while `00:00:00` and `23:59:59` are admitted, so the hour range is 0–23 inclusive. A **DateTime** cell reaches **both**, carries the same `1583-10-16` floor as a Date, and its `'T'` is part of the format rather than tolerated whitespace.

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.TemporalInputFormalCauseDiffTest` — the precision pair, the five-row split, the reality-before-position triple, the seven Time rows, and the four DateTime rows, each on both kernel strategies and the interpreter; the DateTime floor additionally multiplatform in `interpreter … DateGregorianFloorFormalTest`.)*

## §6/§9 supplement: a partial-Date `ValueAsDate` operand is admitted by the READING RULE's scope (kernel, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf208"></a>

> Fold: folded → §6.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-23-12`, **accepted as stated**.

A partial-Date `ValueAsDate` operand may lie **inside a repeatable group**, and admission is decided by the reading rule's own iteration scope, not by the operand's spelling. The persisted condition normalises a relative operand to its absolute path, so the *same* text `ValueAsDate(/Intake/Rows/Partial, FirstDay) > [/Intake/Limit]` is admitted by a rule whose group is `/Intake/Rows` and refused `MVK_NO_WILDCARD` by one at `/Intake`, with a nonrepeatable operand admitted from the form locus as the control. A consumer cannot tell the two apart by reading the rule — which is exactly why the locus has to be stated.

Two refusals ride along, each its own gate. A **starred** operand is `MVK_NO_WILDCARDS_ALLOWED` at **either** locus, so no iteration scope admits one; §7 separately records this operator refusing a group-scope operand `MVK_NO_GROUPS_ALLOWED`, and the two together mean it refuses both wildcard shapes while admitting the bound row read. And a bare partial-Date reference is **not a Date operand at all**: `[PartialTop] > [Limit]` on a `DAY_OPTIONAL` declaration is `MVK_INVALID_DATE_TYPE` — precisely the refusal `ValueAsDate` exists to bridge, so a consumer that cannot produce it leaves the author with no hint about which operation to reach for.

This is [KF204](#kf204)'s locus law on a sixth carrier, and the peer's scope limit is kept: the Date-addition, Date-difference and `DateTime(…)` Date-operand carriers are unmeasured for the locus question, and §7's own finding forbids transferring a locus verdict between carriers in this family.

*(Locked: `validate.laws.ValueAsDateLocusLawsTest` — the two-locus pair with its nonrepeatable control, and the starred/bare-reference gates; operand POSITION stays `ValueAsDatePlacementLawsTest`'s subject and holds at either locus.)*

## §12 supplement: the three direct starred count loops use three distinct partial-validation patterns (kernel, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf209"></a>

> Fold: folded → §12.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `EXP-2026-08-24-01`, **answered by measurement**. The same nine relevance selections were applied to three rules over one two-row `Items*/Qty` column. Dynamic Groovy and generated Java agreed on every exact fired-code set:

| relevance selection | `NumberOfFilledFields` | `NumberOfFilledGroups` | `NumberOfValueInFields` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| field wildcard alone | fires | silent | fires |
| field wildcard + both concrete group rows | silent | silent | fires |
| field wildcard + concrete identifier for that field | fires | silent | fires |
| concrete field identifier + wildcard group | fires | fires | fires |
| all-semantic field wildcard + concrete group rows | fires | silent | fires |
| field wildcard + physical-root concrete group rows | silent | silent | fires |
| both concrete group rows only | silent | silent | silent |
| row 1 only | silent | silent | silent |
| row 2 only | silent | silent | silent |

The competing-account disposition is therefore exact. `NumberOfFilledFields` selects the reduced-universal pattern, rows 1, 3, 4, and 5. `NumberOfValueInFields` selects the existential value-list pattern, rows 1 through 6. `NumberOfFilledGroups` selects none of the four proposed accounts: it fires only on row 4, the concrete field plus wildcard-group shape. This fifth pattern also falsifies the source-derived prediction that the first two operators would share one observable result.

The inert-fixture controls are exact on both strategies: wildcard relevance with two quantities of `11` fires only the filled-field and filled-group rules; two instantiated empty rows fire only the filled-group rule; and no `Items` rows fire none. These controls establish that all three operator routes are live and that the matrix's silence is relevance-driven.

## §6/§11 supplement: interpreted DateRange presentation is declaration-order dependent through shared codegen formats (kernel, 2026-08-24) <a id="kf210"></a>

> Fold: not-foldable — this is a kernel codegen defect rather than field-local DateRange semantics.

Reconciliation of a12-kernel-lean `SPEC-2026-08-24-02`, **superseded by a missing declaration-order control**. The peer's model put interpreted `dd.MM` fields before its interpreted and standard `MM` fields. A typed two-model discriminator keeps the semantic declarations, computations, document, and canonical JSON ingress fixed and reverses only those two declaration blocks. The header ids differ solely to isolate generated-engine caches; `MetaGemeinsameFormate` enumerates field definitions and never reads that id. Both models pass `checkConsistency`; both kernel strategies agree within each model; the results differ across the order:

| input and target | dotted declarations first | month declarations first |
|---|---|---|
| interpreted `MM` source `11/02` into interpreted `MM` target | admitted, `VALUE\|01.11-01.02` | `datumBereichNichtGueltig` on the source |
| standard `MM` source `03/10` into interpreted `MM` target | `VALUE\|01.03-31.10` | `VALUE\|03/10` |

The peer observation is real for its model, but its proposed field-local clauses are not. Neither “an unconfigured interpretation admits wrapping `MM`” nor “an interpreted target chooses the dotted carrier” survives the order reversal.

The source mechanism predicts the separator. `IDateRangeType.getFormatOfDateRange` maps every nonstandard declaration of one direction to a canonical `dd.MM-dd.MM (…)` shared-format key, regardless of that field's declared date format and separator. `MetaGemeinsameFormate` uses a `LinkedHashMap.computeIfAbsent`, while `CodeGenDateRangeTypeImpl` retains the first equal definition's actual `dateFormat` and separator for the emitted runtime format. A dotted field first therefore lends `dd.MM` plus `-` to later equal definitions; an `MM` field first lends `MM` plus `/`. The order-only runtime control is the discriminating case that the field-local account predicts incorrectly.

The independent interpreter stays declaration-local and therefore produces the month-first result under both declaration orders. Encoding the peer clause would replace one measured divergence with an incorrect universal rule. The unresolved conformance work is tracked as [IG141](INTERPRETER-GAPS.md); this reconciliation does not widen it without the full shared-format denominator.

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.DateRangeSharedFormatOrderDiffTest` on both kernel strategies and the independent interpreter, with the exact wrap validity and ordered computation outputs.)*

## §6 supplement: a temporal field's DECLARED FORMAT decides what it is at every gate; its KIND is never read (kernel, both strategies, 2026-08-28) <a id="kf211"></a>

> Fold: pending — extends §6's stored-temporal and comparability accounts; fold together with [KF206](#kf206)'s declaration-tier correction, which it completes.

[KF206](#kf206) established that the temporal format *vocabulary* is kind-independent — a TIME field is refused `HH:mm` and admitted `yyyy-MM-dd` — and stated explicitly that what such a declaration then stores, renders, or is admitted as an operand was a separate question. Measured, it is the **same rule at every tier**. All rows on dynamic Groovy and generated Java, asserted to agree before either meets its expectation, in one model whose cells differ only in kind and declared format.

**The formal channel.**

| declaration | `2024-06-15` | `1583-10-16` | `1583-10-15` | `0000-06-15` | `2024-02-31` | `10:30:00` | `24:00:00` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TIME `yyyy-MM-dd` | admitted | admitted | **`datumFalsch`** | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` |
| DATE `yyyy-MM-dd` | admitted | admitted | `datumFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` |
| DATE_TIME `yyyy-MM-dd` | admitted | admitted | `datumFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` |
| TIME `HH:mm:ss` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | `datumFormatFalsch` | admitted | `datumFormatFalsch` |

**The two separator-free month/day formats read in opposite orders, and that is measured by VALIDITY rather than read off the spelling** *(2026-08-31, on a12-kernel-lean's open assumption)*. The exhaustive grid below asserts that dynamic-Groovy, generated-Java and the interpreter *agree* on each cell; it never pinned **what** they agree on, so the component order was unmeasured here even though both formats sit in the vocabulary. Each pair below is one impossible date in each direction, which is what makes it discriminate:

| declared format | `0229` / `2902` | `0230` / `3002` | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MMdd` | admitted | `datumFormatFalsch` | the leading pair is the **month** — a day-first reading would refuse `0229` for naming month 29 |
| `ddMM` | admitted | `datumFormatFalsch` | the leading pair is the **day** — the mirror argument |

The April rows (`0431`, `3104`) are the same test at a 30-day month, both refused. Note the cause: an out-of-range component in a compact format is `datumFormatFalsch` (format-wrong), not `datumFalsch` (date-wrong), so the classifier treats it as a shape failure rather than a calendar one. *a12-kernel-lean's account of why — one rejection arm for the whole component-omitting family, because no complete date is present to compare against a point-in-time floor — is theirs and is recorded here as their hypothesis, not as a mechanism we measured.* **The STORE direction agrees, measured by a12-kernel-lean rather than here** *(their capture and their oracle, 2026-08-31; cited as their observation, not re-derived)*: one `"11.06.2024"` constant into base-year-2024 targets stores `0611` into `MMdd`, `1106` into `ddMM` and `06-11` into `MM-dd`, both codegen strategies agreeing. So writing follows the same order as reading. **Still unmeasured here** — this estate writes no compact fragment target — and the dashed siblings cannot settle it either way, because they differ from each other in exactly that order.

The two discriminators are independent and that is the point: theirs varies the *spelling* and reads the text back, ours holds the spelling and varies the date's *validity*. Either alone admits a rival account; a round-trip over one estate's own two directions proves only that they agree with each other. Locked in `adapter.laws.TemporalDeclaredFormatGateDiffTest.theSeparatorFreeFormatsReadMonthFirstAndDayFirstRespectively`.

Empty stored text is present and value-free on all four, and the grid behind this table is **exhaustive over the admitted vocabulary**: all **12 formats** × 3 date-bearing kinds are model-legal — 36 of 36 — and every format behaves identically on all three kinds for every value. *(Corrected 2026-09-13: the vocabulary is THIRTEEN since the candidate universe grew a trailing-separator axis, [KF313](#kf313); this grid's 36 cells were exhaustive over the twelve known when it ran and the thirteenth is unmeasured here.)* The members are not listed here on purpose: they are [TEMPORAL-FORMAT-VOCABULARY.md](TEMPORAL-FORMAT-VOCABULARY.md), derived by probing the kernel, and a hand-copy in this paragraph is precisely what went wrong twice. *(Corrected 2026-08-29, twice in one day. First reading: "all 8 formats … 24 of 24", omitting `yyyyMM` — which [KF196](#kf196) already carried, so the denominator had been assembled from the formats this work happened to use rather than queried from the entry that owns them; a peer reviewing our handback caught it. Second reading: "9 … 27 of 27", still short, because KF196's own eleven candidates were themselves hand-picked — deriving the set from the kernel added `MMdd`, `ddMM` and `yyyyMMdd`, named nowhere in this repository. The same edit also retired a false provenance line: the exhaustive grid had been interpreter-only while this entry cited a differential whose kernel coverage was the ISO rows and two controls.)* **Year ZERO takes the format cause while year ONE takes the date cause**, on every date-bearing format and kind: an unreal component is settled before position in time, which is [KF207](#kf207)'s ordering reaching a case that entry did not run. **Two controls, one variable each:** the first three rows hold the declaration fixed and move the kind across every date-bearing kind — they agree, so the kind is not read; rows one and four hold the kind fixed and move the format — they differ on every value, so the declaration is what is read. Comparing two models could not separate these, since two models differ in everything one did not think about.

**The read gates, on the same TIME field declared `yyyy-MM-dd`.** Each admitted arm is paired with a refusal differing in exactly one thing:

| condition | verdict | runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `[TimeAsDate] == [DateAsDate]` | **admitted** | fires on decoded-date equality; a below-floor or clock-spelled cell suppresses the rule and reports only its formal cause |
| `[TimeAsDate] > [DateAsDate]` | **admitted** | fires only when strictly later |
| `[TimeAsTime] == [DateAsDate]` | refused `MVK_INVALID_COMPARE_TO_DATE` | — (the control: same two kinds, only the declared format moved) |
| `YearFromDate(TimeAsDate) == 2024` | **admitted** | fires for every 2024 value |
| `HoursFromTime(TimeAsDate) == 0` | refused `MVK_WRONG_DATE_FORMAT_FOR_OP` | — (the mirror control: the TIME kind's own extractor refuses the TIME field, because its declared format exposes no time component) |
| `DifferenceInDays(TimeAsDate, DateAsDate) == 0` | **admitted** | fires when equal, and also when the operand is EMPTY — the symmetric-zero rule of the difference family |

So the Gregorian floor, direct comparability, component extraction and the difference family all key on the **declared format's component set**. The sharpest single row is the extractor pair: on one cell, `YearFromDate` is admitted and `HoursFromTime` is refused, though the field's kind is TIME.

This corrects [KF207](#kf207) above, whose "because a clock has no position in time" reasoned from the kind: the correct reading is that a *time-format declaration* exposes no position in time, and after [KF206](#kf206) a TIME field need not carry one.

**What this does not say.** Storage and reading only. Rendering, computation targets, and aggregate extrema on such a declaration are untouched here. The typed rulekit surface could express none of the second table's conditions until these rows were measured — `m.date()` threw on a TIME field — and now keys its temporal handles on the declared format instead (API-FINDINGS finding 130). *(All three arrived on 2026-09-07: the rule holds at the `DateRange` endpoint, at the `Date(...)` complete-Year position, and at the aggregate extrema this note excluded — and the same edit found seven read sites where our own converter had stayed keyed on the kind, three of them missed by the sweep that reported the class closed — [KF271](#kf271).)*

**And the READ-GATE table is thin in one specific corner, which is a property of its model rather than of the gates** *(named 2026-09-05, after two independent a12-kernel-lean entries hit it)*. Every row of the second table above is carried on `TimeAsDate` — a TIME field declared `yyyy-MM-dd` — and the model behind it declares **no clock-formatted DATE field at all**: its carriers are TIME-as-date, DATE-as-date, TIME-as-time and the two dotted ones. So the mirror direction is measured only in the *formal* channel (the 12 × 3 vocabulary grid, which does carry it) and in the refusal control; on every READ gate the mirror is **inherited from the classifier rule, not measured**. That inheritance crosses a gate boundary, so it is a scope transfer rather than a consequence. Twice an outside entry landed in that corner and was genuinely new to us: the cross-kind *comparison* mirror, since measured on its own carrier ([KF248](#kf248)), and `HoursFromTime` on a clock-declared DATE — **also measured now, in [KF250](#kf250)**, which takes the extractor pair, the opt-in pre-1900 policy and the declaration schema on that carrier. Expect a third if rendering or a computation target is probed on it; the carrier exists in this estate twice over now, so extending a gate to it no longer needs a new model.

Our interpreter keyed both its formal check and its value canonicalization on the KIND, so a date-declared TIME cell was malformed on every value — suppressing every rule the kernel evaluates on it — and a clock-declared DATE cell was refused a clock. Both are fixed, with the year-zero cause, in [IF314](INTERPRETER-FINDINGS.md#if314); this grid is what turned up the mirror and year zero, neither of which any report named.

*(Locked: `adapter.laws.TemporalDeclaredFormatGateDiffTest` — four declarations × eight stored values, four admitted conditions × six operand pairs, two refusal controls, and a dotted-declaration arm where a decoded date and raw text disagree (`01.07.2024 > 15.06.2024` fires as a date, is silent as text), all on both kernel strategies AND the interpreter; **plus the complete 12-format × 3-kind vocabulary grid**, which asserts model-legality and then kernel-vs-interpreter agreement cell by cell, so the exhaustiveness claim above and its citation are the same artifact. `TemporalFormatVocabularyGuardTest` fails that class if the derived vocabulary ever names a format it omits, which is what keeps "complete" true rather than merely asserted. The year-zero class and the same grid run multiplatform in `interpreter … TemporalDeclaredFormatFormalTest`. Planted mutants: re-declaring the TIME cell as `HH:mm:ss`, and keying the interpreter's classifier on the kind, are both killed.)*

## §9/§11 supplement: `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_IN_RULEGROUP` gates ITERATION, not placement — a rule's and a computation's declaring group are alike free of the field they write (kernel, 2026-08-29) <a id="kf212"></a>

> Fold: pending — a static model-validity (`checkConsistency`) gate; fold into §9's iteration-scope account, whose runtime half [KF19](#kf19) already states that a computation iterates where it WRITES.

The obvious reading of this code — *a rule's error field must be inside its rule group, and a computation's computed field need not, so the two constructs differ* — is wrong in both halves, and both were measured against it. On one model with a non-repeatable target (`/Depot/Stock/StockLevel`), four declaring groups (its own parent, an ancestor, a non-repeatable sibling subtree, a repeatable sibling subtree) and one variable moved per row:

| the construct reads… | rule (error field) | computation (computed field) |
|---|---|---|
| nothing per-row (plain condition / bare constant) | admitted at all four | admitted at all four |
| a per-row field of the REPEATABLE group it is declared in | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_IN_RULEGROUP` | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_IN_RULEGROUP` |
| a per-row field of a repeatable group it is NOT declared in — from an ancestor, or from the target's own parent | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NO_INDEX` | `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NO_INDEX` |

So the gate is **containment under DERIVED ITERATION**: it fires exactly when the construct iterates and the written field does not lie *at or below* the declaring group — containment, not parenthood, so an ancestor of the target satisfies it. The containment demand falls on both constructs identically — measured cell by cell, not inferred from the one matched pair.

**Corrected 2026-08-29 (same day): iteration has a SECOND source, and the tables above cannot see it.** They were published as *"placement alone never refuses either construct"*, which is false. Every row of every table holds the written field **non-repeatable**; with that variable pinned the operand is the only thing left that can vary, so the matrix was blind to the other derivation source — **the written field's own repeatable scope**, which needs no operand at all. Reported as a counterexample by a12-kernel-lean (`SPEC-2026-08-29-01`) and reproduced here as our own measurement on kernel 30.8.1; a bare string constant computed into `/Depot/Shipments/Units` is **refused** from the unrelated fixed `/Depot/Policy` and from the unrelated repeatable `/Depot/Returns`, and **admitted** from `/Depot/Shipments` itself and from the ancestor `/Depot`. The two sources are independent: either one alone derives iteration.

**The two constructs are not symmetric on that second source, though they share the gate.** A rule's error field must be REFERENCED by its condition (`MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_REFERENCED`, measured here), so a repeatable error field is necessarily also a per-row operand and the two sources collapse into one; only a computation can pair a constant operand with a repeating target. That is why the counterexample could only be found on the computation side, and it is the correction to the earlier "identical for both constructs" phrasing: identical on the *gate*, not on which sources each construct can exhibit alone. The discriminating row is the second: it holds the declaring group and the written field fixed and moves only the operand, which is what separates this from the operand-admission law ([KF19](#kf19)'s neighbour, `ComputationOperandScopeLawsTest`) — there the target's scope decides which operands are *readable*, here an already-readable operand decides whether the *written* field must move.

**The index declaration is controlled, because on the neighbouring axis it decides the verdict.** `ComputationOperandScopeLawsTest` measured that declaring a sibling repeatable group's index field flips its operand verdict, so a per-row table built only on an index-keyed group measures siblinghood and index-keying at once. Re-measuring row 2 on a repeatable group carrying the same key field but **not declaring it as the index** returns `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_IN_RULEGROUP` for both constructs unchanged: the containment demand is the iteration's, not the index declaration's.

Consumer-visible consequence: the `computation add` spec's optional `group` still needs no containment pre-check — the client cannot see either derivation source without parsing the operation and resolving the target's repeatability, and both refusals are the kernel's to report with the same code. **The CLI and the library are nonetheless stricter than the kernel on the rule side, at two loci** (source-verified): `Rule.Builder.build()` refuses an error field outside the rule group (`RK_ERROR_FIELD_OUTSIDE_GROUP`, the published-API locus the [MVK-LEDGER](MVK-LEDGER.md) row cites) and `RuleAddCommand` repeats the check on the spec — while table row 1 shows the kernel admits exactly that pair. Left standing: narrowing a live refusal is a contract change for `rule add`, not a wording fix. It is a `pre-checked` over-rejection in the ledger's own sense of that bucket, and the row now says so.

*Hypothesis, not actionable, and not measured here:* the refusal may also be load-bearing for `Rule.errorEntityRelPath()`, whose substring arithmetic (`"../" + errorField.substring(group.length() + 1)`, source-read 2026-08-29) has no defined result without containment — the reason KERNEL-INTEGRATION-NOTES records for it. If that holds, `EntityPath.relativize` is the general replacement and the refusal is removable rather than inherent. What would settle it is one authoring probe of the uncontained pair through `Rule.Builder` with the check lifted; nobody has run it.

**The operand-bearing route obeys the same gate, cell for cell — measured 2026-08-29 on a12-kernel-lean's `SPEC-2026-08-29-02`.** A star aggregate over a sibling repeatable group (`Sum(/Depot/Returns*/Units)`) computed into the repeatable `/Depot/Shipments/Units` returns the *identical* four verdicts as the bare constant: admitted at the target's own parent and at the ancestor root, `MVK_ERROR_FIELD_NOT_IN_RULEGROUP` at the unrelated fixed subtree and at the starred source's own group. The row-for-row match is what separates the two accounts of the ancestor admission — "the star operand earns it" versus "containment alone decides" — since only the second predicts a match. It also corrects the §11 sibling-star entry's phrasing, which measured that shape only at the target's own parent and so read as the sole admitted placement.

**The consequence an author meets first: the declaring group is the operand's RENDERING BASE, so moving a computation upward silently re-points a relative operand — and misattributes on two different codes.** A stale `../Primary*/Candidate` left unchanged refuses `MVK_INVALID_ENTITY` when the walk lands inside the tree on a group that does not exist (declaring group `/Warehouse/Yard`), and `MVK_TOO_MANY_PARENT_GROUPS` when it walks off the top of the model instead (declaring group `/Warehouse`, the root) — an arity refusal that pre-empts resolution. Re-spelling the operand for the new base admits the same placement, which is the control that keeps both refusals the spelling's rather than the placement's. a12-kernel-lean reports only the first code; its ancestor was not a root. *(Locked: `cli … ComputationDeclaringGroupCliTest.aStaleRelativeOperandMisattributesOnTwoCodesWhenTheDeclaringGroupMovesUp`. It is a TEXT-operand fact, which is why the CLI is where it is locked: `Computation.draft` renders through `new DslRenderer(language, groupPath)` over model-bound absolute refs (source-read 2026-08-29), so a typed operand is re-based by construction and carries no spelling that can go stale.)*

**Resolved 2026-09-15 — the CONSTRUCT carries the asymmetry, and the declaring group's own repeatability carries none of it.** Two published sets disagreed about the second derivation source and neither could say why: a computation with a bare constant into a per-row target outside its declaring group is REFUSED (`NonIteratingComputationFreedomLawsTest`, from a FIXED declaring group), while a rule reaching its per-row error field through a non-repeatable ancestor, outside its declaring group, is ADMITTED (`RootOnlyErrorTargetIterationLawsTest`'s fixed-root control, from a REPEATABLE one). Both the construct and the declaring group's repeatability moved between those rows. The 2×2 on one model moves one at a time: rule ADMITTED at both declaring groups, computation REFUSED at both. **So a computation's per-row COMPUTED FIELD derives iteration on its own and a rule's per-row ERROR FIELD does not** — the gate is shared, the sources are not, and the earlier sentence that only a computation can EXHIBIT the second source alone understated it: a rule cannot exhibit it at all.
